Many spatial panel outcomes are ordered categories: credit ratings, survey
scales, damage levels, land-use intensity. `psoprobit()` fits the spatial
ordered probit model. It uses the same arguments as `psprobit()` (see
`vignette("getting-started")`), so this vignette concentrates on what is
specific to ordered outcomes.

```{r}
library(panelspatialprobit)
```

## The model

The latent model is the same as in the binary case,

$$z_t = \rho W z_t + X_t\beta + W X_t\theta + \alpha + \varepsilon_t,
\qquad \varepsilon_t \sim N(0, I_N),$$

and the observed category is $y_{it} = j$ when
$\kappa_{j-1} < z_{it} \le \kappa_j$, for $j = 1, \dots, J$, with
$\kappa_0 = -\infty$ and $\kappa_J = +\infty$.

**Identification.** The model includes an intercept, so the first cut-point is
fixed at $\kappa_1 = 0$, and the free cut-points are
$0 < \kappa_2 < \dots < \kappa_{J-1}$ (named `cut[2|3]`, `cut[3|4]`, ...). This
is the parameterisation of `MCMCpack::MCMCoprobit`. Packages such as
`MASS::polr` and `ordinal::clm` drop the intercept and estimate all $J - 1$
thresholds instead; `summary()` reports the thresholds in that
parameterisation too, $\zeta_j = \kappa_j - \beta_0$.

The response can be an ordered factor, a factor (its level order is used) or
integer codes. Every category must occur in the data.

## Example

We simulate $J = 4$ categories on a 10 × 10 grid observed over 5 periods:

```{r}
W <- psp_weights(rook_weights(10, 10), style = "W")
d <- sim_psprobit(W, T = 5, beta = c(0.2, 1, -0.8), rho = 0.5, sigma_alpha = 0.6,
                  cutpoints = c(0.8, 1.6), seed = 7)
d$y <- factor(d$y, labels = c("none", "low", "medium", "high"), ordered = TRUE)
table(d$y)
```

```{r}
fit <- psoprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d, index = c("id", "time"), W = W,
                 control = psp_control(iter = 3000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2,
                                       seed = 1, progress = FALSE))
summary(fit)
```

The truth is $\beta = (0.2, 1, -0.8)$, $\rho = 0.5$, $\sigma_\alpha = 0.6$ and
cut-points $(0, 0.8, 1.6)$.

## Impacts per category

A regressor moves probability mass between categories: if it raises the latent
outcome, the top categories become more likely and the bottom ones less
likely. Impacts are therefore reported **per category** and, for each
regressor and effect type, sum to zero over the categories.

```{r}
imp <- fit$impacts
s <- summary(imp)
s[s$variable == "x1" & s$effect == "total", c("category", "mean", "q2.5", "q97.5")]
sum(s$mean[s$variable == "x1" & s$effect == "total"])
```

The options of `psp_impacts()` (`type = "unit"`, `by_period = TRUE`,
`scale = "lesage_pace"`) work as for binary models.

## Predicted probabilities

`predict(type = "prob")` returns an $NT \times J$ matrix of posterior mean
category probabilities, in the row order of the data; `type = "class"` returns
the most probable category.

```{r}
head(round(predict(fit), 3))
psp_classification(fit)$confusion
```

## The cut-point sampler

Updating the cut-points one at a time given the latent values (Albert and Chib
1993) mixes slowly when there are many observations, because each cut-point is
squeezed between the latent values of the neighbouring categories. The default
sampler (`cutpoint_sampler = "transform"`) adds a joint Metropolis–Hastings move
that shifts a cut-point and rescales the latent values of the two adjacent
categories with it (Liu and Sabatti 2000), so the cut-point can move far in
one step. Its step size is tuned during warm-up; the acceptance rates after
warm-up are stored in the fit:

```{r}
fit$cut_accept
```

`cutpoint_sampler = "albert_chib"` uses the Gibbs step alone. Both samplers
target the same posterior and pass simulation-based calibration; the
transformation move gives a higher effective sample size per second for the
cut-points, by up to two orders of magnitude for interior cut-points (see
`vignette("validation")`).

## Priors on the cut-points

The default prior is $N(0, 10^2)$ on each free cut-point, restricted to the
ordering constraint. `psp_priors(cutpoints = prior_flat())` uses a flat prior,
as `MCMCpack::MCMCoprobit` does.

## References

polychotomous response data. *Journal of the American Statistical
Association* 88, 669–679.

LeSage, J. P., Pace, R. K., Lam, N., Campanella, R. and Liu, X. (2011). New
Orleans business recovery in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina. *Journal of
the Royal Statistical Society A* 174, 1007–1027.

Liu, J. S. and Sabatti, C. (2000). Generalised Gibbs sampler and multigrid
Monte Carlo for Bayesian computation. *Biometrika* 87, 353–369.
